scenes.text: In 2021, GM recalled every Chevy Bolt it had ever sold. The battery cells were faulty, and fixing them cost nearly two billion dollars. Hyundai had to swap the batteries in eighty-two thousand cars.

I'm Catalyst, and I check battery material before it's made into cells. This is an anode under a microscope. Grey is graphite. Orange is silicon, which holds far more lithium but swells every charge. Blue is the space the lithium moves through. If the mix is off, lithium can plate out as metal, and in the worst case short the cell and start a fire.

When a batch arrives, I compare it with what the supplier promised. Each row shows how far one measurement has moved. This batch says investigate, so it's held for a closer look. The tabs explain it for each role, from operator to manager.
You can also give me a single image. I'll tell you which batch it looks closest to, and how sure I am. If it sits outside even that batch, I flag it as unfamiliar.
You can check my work. Open any image and turn on the overlay to see which pixels I counted as silicon and which as pores.
Every comparison is saved with a fingerprint of its images and settings. Press verify, and I check that nothing has changed. And if a batch turns out bad, there's one more button.

Last, two experiments we're still testing. The first estimates what the differences I found could mean for the cell, like its capacity or how fast it can charge. It also shows the worst case, and what would rule it out.
The second turns the measurements into a 3D anode you can charge. Charge it too fast, and lithium plates out as metal.
After eight hundred cycles, the silicon has cracked.
That's me, Catalyst. Send me your next batch. Made by Team Batch Size 2.
